paragraphs: It is a very common opinion, especially in aristocratic countries, that the great social equality prevailing in democracies eventually makes the private soldier independent of the officer and so destroys the bond of discipline. This is a mistake, for there are two kinds of discipline, and it is important not to confuse them. When the officer is a noble and the soldier a serf, one rich and the other poor, the first educated and strong and the second ignorant and weak, the strictest bond of obedience can easily be established between them. The soldier is, so to speak, broken in to military discipline before he enters the army; or rather, military discipline is nothing but a heightening of social servitude. In aristocratic armies the soldier soon becomes deaf to everything but the orders of his superiors. He acts without reflection, triumphs without enthusiasm and dies without complaint. In this state he is no longer a man, but he is still a most formidable animal trained for war.

A democratic people must give up hope of ever getting from soldiers the blind, minute, submissive and unvarying obedience that an aristocratic people can impose on them without difficulty. The state of society does not prepare them for it, and the nation might risk losing its natural advantages if it tried to acquire advantages of this particular kind by artificial means. Among democratic communities, military discipline should not try to destroy the free play of the faculties. All discipline can do is direct it. The obedience it instills is less exact, but it is more eager and more intelligent. It is rooted in the will of the one who obeys; it rests not only on his instinct but on his reason. As a result, it will often tighten of its own accord when danger demands it. The discipline of an aristocratic army tends to slacken in war, because that discipline rests on habit, and war disrupts habit. The discipline of a democratic army, by contrast, grows stronger within sight of the enemy, because every soldier then sees clearly that he must be silent and obedient in order to win.

The nations that have achieved the greatest feats of war knew no other discipline than the kind I am speaking of. Among the ancients, only freemen and citizens were admitted into the armies. They differed little from one another and were used to treating each other as equals. In this respect the armies of antiquity may be called democratic, though they came out of the bosom of aristocracy. As a result, a kind of brotherly familiarity prevailed in those armies between officers and men. Plutarch’s lives of great commanders offer convincing examples. The soldiers were in the constant habit of speaking freely to their general, and the general listened to whatever the soldiers had to say and answered it. They were kept in order by words and example far more than by compulsion or punishment. The general was as much their companion as their chief. I do not know whether the soldiers of Greece and Rome ever carried the fine points of military discipline to the same degree of perfection as the Russians have. But this did not prevent Alexander from conquering Asia, or Rome from conquering the world.
